How a Small Team Shipped a Compiler

By Ada Lovelace

When the team began work on the compiler, nobody believed that four engineers could produce a production-quality toolchain in a single year. The project started as an experiment in incremental delivery: every week the compiler had to compile something real, even if that something was a single arithmetic expression. That constraint changed the architecture. Instead of building an elaborate intermediate representation first and a parser later, the team built a thin vertical slice and let the representation grow with the language.

The second lesson was about testing. The team wrote hundreds of small programs that were expected to fail to compile, and every one of them carried a diagnostic message that a person could understand. Error messages became the user interface, and the team treated them with the same care as generated code. A confusing message, they argued, is a bug in the compiler just as surely as a miscompiled branch is.

Finally, the team invested early in reproducible builds. Read the build notes for the details. The compiler shipped on time, with fewer defects than the previous project, and the team attributed the result to the weekly slice, the diagnostics, and the builds.
